name: LuaJIT
baseline: QuickJS (cross-language, same algorithms); also PUC Lua (see caveats)
workload: plb2: nqueen (15-queens), 1500x1500 matmul, 4000 sudokus, bedcov interval overlap, each implemented with the same algorithm per language; elapsed seconds, lower is better.
claimed_speedup: LuaJIT 2.1 vs QuickJS 23-12-09 on Apple M1 (seconds): nqueen 5.31 vs 59.04, matmul 2.66 vs 135.66, sudoku 4.48 vs 67.55, bedcov 10.52 vs 37.56 (ratios derived from page data: about 11x, 51x, 15x, 3.6x).
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Pro (timed with hyperfine)
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1 language level (plus extensions), so newer Lua 5.2-5.4 features are missing; JIT tiers are unavailable on platforms that forbid runtime code generation, where only the interpreter (still fast) can be used.
caveats: Primary evidence compares against QuickJS, not PUC Lua, because plb2 has no PUC Lua row; plb2 is tier B (independent suite, code public, CPU stated, but LuaJIT build flags not stated). Older independent data against PUC Lua: the 2015 Scriptorium shootout (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/r-lyeh-archived/scriptorium/HEAD/README.md, AMD A10 3.8 GHz, Windows 7, VS2015) lists luajit 0.111 s, luajit-nojit 0.521 s and Lua 1.341 s on a recursive Fibonacci test. The LuaJIT repo itself carries no benchmark numbers (the project's performance page luajit.org is not reachable from here). Last commit date read from the GitHub commits page for branch v2.1.
found_via: GitHub: attractivechaos/plb2 README opened while checking shootouts for embeddable scripting engines; query 'embeddable scripting language C++ faster than Lua benchmark github'

name: LuaJIT Remake (Deegen-generated Lua interpreter)
baseline: PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter and LuaJIT interpreter
workload: Geometric mean over the repo's luabench suite of Lua benchmarks, interpreter-only, GC disabled in all implementations for fairness.
claimed_speedup: 34.6% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter and 185% faster than the official PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter (geometric average over all benchmarks, each repeated 5 times).
hardware: Intel i7-12700H laptop, 32GB DDR4 (stated in README footnote)
tradeoffs: Work in progress: Lua 5.1 interpreter only (JIT tiers not finished), x86-64 Linux only, package library (require/module) and some stdlib functions missing; built via docker with a custom ljr-build script.
caveats: First-party README claim; benchmark scripts (luabench, run_bench.sh) are public but compiler and flags for the build and for the baselines are not stated, hence tier C. GC is not implemented in this project and was switched off in the baselines to compare, so real workloads with GC will see a smaller gap. Not production-ready per its own caveats. Author blog posts with details (sillycross.github.io) were not reachable from here.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Lua interpreter fork faster than PUC Lua 5.4 github benchmark speedup embeddable'; README opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Luau
workload: Interpreter dispatch loop, table library, string library and garbage collector sweep, as described in the project's performance guide.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter 'noticeably faster than Lua 5.x (including Lua 5.4 ... doesn't come close)'; table.sort about 4x speedup on average; table insert/remove/move 3x and more vs un-tuned versions; paged GC sweeper 2-3x faster than Lua/LuaJIT linked-list sweep and 16 bytes less per object; table length 50+% faster.
compiler_and_flags: Interpreter tuned for Clang and recent MSVC (per guide); no flags stated
stars_or_usage: 5.9k stars; scripting layer of Roblox, also adopted in commercial games per README
tradeoffs: Derived from Lua 5.1 with its own type annotations and a sandboxing model (safeenv via luaL_sandbox) that the fastest paths rely on; API mostly Lua 5.1 compatible with caveats; interpreter-first design, JIT/native codegen is optional and not available everywhere.
caveats: First-party documentation page with ratios but no workload list, hardware, compiler flags or raw numbers, so tier C. The repo has a bench/ directory (bench.py, micro_tests, gc) but no checked-in result tables that I could find. Several gains (fastcall builtins, safeenv) require the sandboxed global setup. Some comparisons are against Lua 5.1 baseline structures and 'un-tuned' library versions rather than stock PUC 5.4 library functions.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Lua interpreter fork faster than PUC Lua 5.4 github benchmark speedup embeddable' (surfaced the Luau performance guide); guide read from luau-lang/site repo via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: PrimJS
workload: Octane benchmark suite (version 9 scoring), 15 sub-benchmarks, QuickJS vs PrimJS template interpreter + tracing GC.
claimed_speedup: Overall Octane score 3735 vs 2904 for QuickJS (about 28% higher); e.g. RayTrace 2751 vs 1273, EarleyBoyer 4270 vs 2284, NavierStokes 4166 vs 2640, PdfJS 6642 vs 4236; a few rows are lower (CodeLoad 16992 vs 18137, MandreelLatency 9587 vs 9680).
compiler_and_flags: gn args: enable_quickjs_debugger=false target_cpu="arm64" target_os="mac" is_debug=false enable_optimize_with_O2=true; enable_primjs_snapshot, enable_compatible_mm, enable_tracing_gc left at default true; compiler not named
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; JS engine of ByteDance's Lynx framework
tradeoffs: QuickJS fork (ES2019) with a template interpreter, tracing GC instead of reference counting, CDP debugger and initial WebAssembly; uses gn/ninja and a hab dependency sync rather than a simple drop-in C file set.
caveats: First-party numbers; Octane code is public and CPU and build args are stated, but the compiler is not named, hence C (close to A). README states the snapshot, compatible memory management and tracing GC are enabled by default only on arm64 Android, iOS and macOS (pre-generated embedded.S); on Linux and non-arm64 targets they are off, so the gain may not carry over. Independent CI shootout (ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark/HEAD/README.md) shows primjs slightly below QuickJS (macos-arm64 1694 vs 1761; ubuntu 737 vs 1217), though its build configuration there is unknown.
found_via: WebSearch: 'JavaScript engine faster than QuickJS embeddable benchmark github small footprint' led to the ahaoboy shootout listing primjs; README and docs/benchmark.md fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: V8
baseline: QuickJS (and Duktape in the same table)
workload: Octane/v8-v7 subset (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run as a standalone shell by CI on three OSes; plb2 adds nqueen/matmul/sudoku/bedcov via Node.
claimed_speedup: Suite score: v8 48107 vs QuickJS 1217 on ubuntu, 64220 vs 1761 on macos-arm64, 46932 vs 1067 on windows (derived from page data: about 40x, 36x, 44x). In plb2 (Apple M1) Node 21.5.0 nqueen 3.73 s vs QuickJS 59.04 s and matmul 2.88 s vs 135.66 s.
hardware: CI runners (ubuntu, macos-arm64, windows sections of the README, results dated 10/5/2026); CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 25.3k stars (official mirror); engine of Chromium and Node.js
tradeoffs: Embeddable C++ API, but large (shell build listed at 66M total, score per MB 729 vs QuickJS 1190), complex build system (gn/depot_tools), JIT requires writable-executable memory so it is not usable on locked-down platforms; much higher memory and startup cost than QuickJS or Duktape.
caveats: Third-party shootout run by CI on GitHub-hosted runners; CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated and the engine binaries come from prebuilt per-engine build repos (e.g. ahaoboy/v8-build), so this is tier B rather than A. The suite is an Octane/v8-v7 subset (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) scored over a fixed time budget. JIT engine vs interpreter-only baseline, so the comparison trades footprint and startup for peak speed. GitHub repo is a mirror of chromium.googlesource.com. plb2 numbers are from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/attractivechaos/plb2/HEAD/README.md (Node and Bun, not a bare V8 shell).
found_via: WebSearch: 'JavaScript engine faster than QuickJS embeddable benchmark github small footprint' (ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark); repo page opened on github.com

name: Wren
baseline: Lua (5.x), with LuaJIT (-joff), Python and Ruby as comparators
workload: Repo benchmark scripts (test/benchmark: binary_trees, fib, for, method_call) implemented identically in Wren, Lua, Python and Ruby.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Wren is fast ... help Wren compete with other dynamic languages'. Performance page (snippet only): method_call Wren 0.12 s vs Lua 0.35 s; with Wren 0.4 method_call 0.079 s vs LuaJIT 2.1 -joff 0.090 s; but fib Lua 5.4 0.090 s vs Wren 0.148 s and binary_trees Lua 5.4 0.138 s vs Wren 0.144 s.
tradeoffs: Class-based, fiber-concurrent language with an easy C API; compiles as C99 or C++98 and later; small standard library.
caveats: Snippet only: wren.io is blocked here (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so the numbers come from a WebSearch summary of the performance page and the muxup.com 'Updating Wren's benchmarks' post, neither of which I could open; treat as unverified. Result is mixed against Lua: faster on method dispatch, level or slower on fib and binary_trees in the 2023 numbers. The 2015 Scriptorium shootout (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/r-lyeh-archived/scriptorium/HEAD/README.md) lists Wren at 1.997 s vs Lua 1.341 s on recursive Fibonacci (slower than Lua). Repo contains the benchmark scripts but no result tables; issue #538 notes the official comparison originally covered only Python and Ruby.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Wren scripting language performance benchmarks vs Lua LuaJIT Python Ruby fib method_call binary_trees'; README and test/benchmark README opened on raw.githubusercontent.com

name: sol2
baseline: Other C++ Lua binding libraries (LuaBridge, OOLua, Kaguya, luwra, Selene, SWIG, tolua++ and others); floor is the plain Lua C API
workload: Per-operation overhead of binding layers over the Lua C API (member function call, userdata variable access, table get/set, multi-return and others) measured with nonius in the lua-bindings-shootout repo.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Fastest in the land (see: sol2 bar in graph)'; benchmarks page: sol 'seems to take the cake in most categories for speed'. The page has graphs only, no numeric table.
compiler_and_flags: All libraries compiled against a DLL build of Lua 5.3.3, no link-time optimization (per page); compiler and flags otherwise not stated
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 binding for Lua, LuaJIT and others; heavy template use means long compile times; its fast paths (c_call and disabled type checks) trade safety for speed.
caveats: Evidence is first-party graphs from 2018 (page dated May 17th, 2018) with the author's own shootout; no numbers on the page. Approximate values I read off the member-function-call bar chart image in lua-bindings-shootout (benchmark_results/member function call.png): plain_c about 115 ns, sol3 about 135, oolua about 145, sol2 about 150, luwra about 205, luabridge about 420, old sol about 425, toluapp about 590 (approximate, not text on the page). A newer first-party chart in the LuaBridge3 README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kunitoki/LuaBridge3/HEAD/README.md, image Images/benchmarks.png) shows Sol3 slower than LuaBridge3 on member function call (356.9 vs 152.4 ns), so the ranking depends on version and safety settings. Binding-layer overhead, not script execution speed; baseline is not in the category list. The shootout repo README states no hardware or compiler flags.
found_via: WebSearch: 'embeddable scripting language C++ faster than Lua benchmark github' (lua binding benchmarks); sol2 README, benchmarks.rst and shootout PNGs fetched

name: LuaBridge3
baseline: Sol3 (sol2) and vanilla LuaBridge (C++ Lua binding overhead over the plain Lua C API)
workload: Per-operation binding overhead in nanoseconds across about 35 cases (global/table access, free and member function calls, userdata properties, shared-pointer ownership, multi-return, lambda captures, converters), each run in isolation with maximum safety settings.
claimed_speedup: README chart (nanoseconds, lower is better): member function call 152.4 vs Sol3 356.9; userdata variable access 70.2 vs Sol3 299.9 and vanilla LuaBridge 269.3; derived method call 91.8 vs Sol3 260.5; c function 44.2 vs Sol3 116.2; but table get 29.1 vs Sol3 17.9 (slower) and table chained get 69.6 vs Sol3 28.0 (slower).
compiler_and_flags: All libraries compiled together with the benchmark executable so inlining and LTO apply; compiler and flags not stated
tradeoffs: Dependency-free binding that works with PUC Lua, LuaJIT, Luau and Ravi; supports many C++17/20/23 std types, lambdas and multiple inheritance; works with or without exceptions.
caveats: First-party chart embedded in the README as an image (Images/benchmarks.png); the numbers I quote were read from that image, not from page text. No hardware, compiler or flags stated. Mixed results: Sol3 is faster on several table get/set cases and vanilla LuaBridge is faster on a few call cases. README itself says it 'competes directly with sol2' rather than beating it everywhere. Baseline is not in the category list.
found_via: WebSearch: 'embeddable scripting language C++ faster than Lua benchmark github' (Lua binding results); README and benchmarks.png fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Terra
workload: Scriptorium: recursive Fibonacci in 50 scripting-language implementations, seconds, lower is better.
claimed_speedup: terra 0.121 s vs Lua 1.341 s (page shows 'x11.0' relative Lua speed; about 11x derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Compiled on VS2015 RC if possible, VS2013 elsewhere (per page)
tradeoffs: Terra is a statically typed low-level language JIT-compiled through LLVM and hosted inside Lua, not a faster Lua interpreter: speedups only apply to code rewritten as Terra, and it needs LLVM. I did not verify a C or C++ embedding API.
caveats: Single micro-benchmark (recursive fib), dated July 2015, run on Windows 7; the page itself says 'Take it with a grain of salt'. Entry is an independent shootout (tier B), but comparison is Terra-typed code against dynamically typed Lua. Peer-reviewed Terra paper (PLDI 2013) was not reachable here. Scriptorium repo is archived (r-lyeh-archived).
